message.content:
Here’s a concise overview of the key properties of hydrogen (H), covering its most commonly referenced characteristics: | Property | Value | Notes | |----------|-------|-------| | **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. | | **Symbol** | H | From the Greek *hydro* (water). | | **Common isotope** | ^1H (protium) | 99.98 % natural abundance. | | **Other stable isotopes** | ^2H (deuterium, 0.015 %)
^3H (tritium, ~10⁻⁵ %) | Tritium is radioactive (β‑emitter, half‑life ≈12.32 yr). | | **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Weighted by natural isotope abundances. | | **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. | | **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. | | **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy to remove the single valence electron. | | **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy released when an electron is added. | | **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | At 1 atm. | | **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | At 1 atm. | | **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | Extremely low; lighter than air. | | **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Ideal gas approximation. | | **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy required to break H₂ into two H atoms. | | **Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f)** | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) | For elemental hydrogen in its standard state. | | **Standard entropy (S°)** | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | At 298 K, 1 atm. | | **Standard Gibbs free energy of formation (ΔG°f)** | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ | By definition for elemental hydrogen. | | **Typical oxidation states** | +1 (most common) | Forms H⁺ in acids; also +1 in hydrides (e.g., NaH). | | **Common compounds** | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. | Hydrogen is a key component of many molecules. | ### Quick Takeaways - **Lightest element**: Hydrogen has the lowest atomic mass and density of all elements. - **Highly reactive**: Its single valence electron makes it eager to share or lose electrons, forming covalent bonds or ions. - **Isotopic significance**: Deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research and as tracers in chemistry and biology. - **Energy relevance**: Hydrogen’s high ionization energy and electronegativity make it a strong oxidizer in many contexts. Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property (e.g., spectroscopic data, phase diagram, or applications in industry).
